rationale: Ecclesiastes describes making gardens and planting every kind of fruit tree. Genesis describes God planting Eden's garden and causing trees good for food to spring up. The concrete shared pattern is a planted garden with edible trees; the royal experiment is not identified with Eden or assigned its tree of life.

relationship: Irrigation used literally and as a teaching image
rationale: Ecclesiastes constructs water pools to irrigate growing woodland. Sirach compares the speaker to a river channel entering a garden and speaks of watering a garden bed, before applying the flowing image to instruction. Both picture directed water nourishing cultivated growth; Sirach's figurative channel is not claimed to be the same physical pool or woodland.

Ecclesiastes includes a time to keep and a time to throw away. The storm narrative gives a concrete occasion for discarding previously useful cargo and ship's tackle. This illustrates the disposal half of the saying under danger, without making the whole time catalogue a prediction of that voyage.

relationship: Contrasting periods of war and peace
rationale: Ecclesiastes places a time of war beside a time of peace. David recounts his great wars and God's promise of rest, peace and quietness in Solomon's days. Chronicles supplies a particular contrast between such periods, while the separate love-and-hate pair is not assigned to either king.

Ecclesiastes names warmth as a benefit when two lie down together. When clothing does not warm David, his attendants seek a woman to lie with him, and Abishag keeps him warm. The narrative concretely shares the bodily-warmth benefit; its explicit statement that David did not know her is preserved rather than making the comparison sexual.

relationship: Stillbirth described through absence of light
rationale: In context Ecclesiastes speaks of a stillborn child whose departure and covered name are in darkness. Job compares his wished-for rest with a miscarriage or infants who never saw light. Both use the stillborn child's separation from the light of life in reflections on suffering; Job does not supply the separate detail of a name covered in darkness.

Ecclesiastes says it is unwise to ask why former days were better. Numbers recounts Israel's claim that it was well with them in Egypt and rebukes their disobedient lament over leaving. The narrative is a particular instance of a criticized favorable comparison with the past, without claiming every recollection of earlier days is wrong.

relationship: Oil on the head alongside enjoyed provision
rationale: Ecclesiastes urges an oiled head in a setting of glad eating and drinking. The psalm joins a prepared table, a head enriched with oil and an excellent cup. Both associate head-anointing with enjoyed provision; the psalm does not mention the white garments or identify a shared ritual.

Ecclesiastes warns that splitting wood brings danger. Deuteronomy gives the concrete case of an axe's iron slipping while wood is cut, killing a neighbor and exposing the cutter to an avenger. Both recognize woodcutting's dangers, while the legal example distinguishes the neighbor's immediate injury from the cutter's ensuing danger.

relationship: Serpent danger and the limits of charming
rationale: Ecclesiastes says a bite without a whispered charm leaves no advantage for the charmer. The psalm pictures a deaf asp refusing to hear enchanters or a wise person's spell. Both connect dangerous serpents with ineffective charming; the proverb's absent charm and the psalm's refused charm are distinct circumstances.

Ecclesiastes says wine gladdens the living while speaking of bread and money. The psalm similarly says wine gladdens the human heart, beside oil brightening the face and bread making the heart firm. This is a particular shared description of wine's gladness, without using the psalm to explain everything listening to money.
